abstract: We report an efficient electrocatalyst utilizing non-noble metals consisting of Cu and Sn supported on nitrogen-doped graphene (NG) for reduction of CO2 over a wide potential range. The CuSn alloy nanoparticles (NPs) on NG were prepared through a hydrothermal method followed by pyrolysis under nitrogen atmosphere to achieve a uniform dispersion of the alloy NPs. The CuSn NP (Cu/Sn ratio of 0.175) decorated NG catalyst performed electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 into C1 products at a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of nearly 93% at an overpotential of 1.0 V vs. RHE, considerably higher than that of the Cu and Sn counterparts, i. e., 32% and 58%, respectively. The enhanced catalytic activity could be attributed to the collaboration between the CuSn alloy and Sn metal. The firstprinciples density functional theory (DFT) simulation results indicate that the CuSn bimetal alloy nanoparticles enable more H atoms to participate in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 and exhibit an improved CO2 capture performance. In addition, the CuSn alloy having a lower barrier than that of Sn metal can accelerate the CO2 reduction process. This study presents the strategy that utilizes low-cost non-noble metals as highly efficient electrocatalysts for aqueous reduction of CO2.

sections.heading: CuSn Alloy Nanoparticles on Nitrogen-Doped Graphene for Electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction
sections.text:
Wei Xiong,[a, b] Jian Yang,[c] Ling Shuai,[d] Yang Hou,*[c] Ming Qiu,*[d] Xinyong Li,[a] and Michael K. H. Leung*[b]
We report an efficient electrocatalyst utilizing non-noble metals consisting of Cu and Sn supported on nitrogen-doped graphene (NG) for reduction of CO2 over a wide potential range. The CuSn alloy nanoparticles (NPs) on NG were prepared through a hydrothermal method followed by pyrolysis under nitrogen atmosphere to achieve a uniform dispersion of the alloy NPs. The CuSn NP (Cu/Sn ratio of 0.175) decorated NG catalyst performed electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 into C1 products at a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of nearly 93% at an overpotential of 1.0 V vs. RHE, considerably higher than that of the Cu and Sn counterparts, i. e., 32% and 58%, respectively. The enhanced catalytic activity could be attributed to the collaboration between the CuSn alloy and Sn metal. The firstprinciples density functional theory (DFT) simulation results indicate that the CuSn bimetal alloy nanoparticles enable more H atoms to participate in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 and exhibit an improved CO2 capture performance. In addition, the CuSn alloy having a lower barrier than that of Sn metal can accelerate the CO2 reduction process. This study presents the strategy that utilizes low-cost non-noble metals as highly efficient electrocatalysts for aqueous reduction of CO2.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The conversion of carbon dioxide gas into valuable compounds by electrocatalytic reduction reaction is considered as a potential strategy for mitigating excess CO2 levels in the atmosphere and realizing an artificial carbon cycle synthetically.[1] In recent years, many catalysts have been developed for the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), including metals,
[2] metal oxides,[3] transition-metal chalcogenides,[4] metal-organic frameworks,[5] carbon-based materials,[6] etc. Among them, copper (Cu) and tin (Sn) are effective candidates, due to their low cost and unique activities.[7] By employing Cu and Sn as the electrocatalysts, CO2 can be reduced to CO, formic acid and other hydrocarbons at mild condition. However, the CO2RR is generally difficult due to the thermodynamic stability, resulting in very sluggish reaction
kinetics during electrocatalytic reduction. In addition, the conversion of CO2 usually competes against the evolution of hydrogen, which significantly decreases the selectivity of reduced carbon products.[8] Highly active, selective and stable electrocatalysts are still required to meet the criteria for practical applications of CO2RR.
Different strategies have been developed to increase the activity of electrocatalysts including alloying, shape control, surface modification, element doping and oxidative treatment etc.[9] Among them, alloying has been regarded as one of the effective approaches as the bimetallic alloying may change the conventional electronic and/or geometric structures and ensemble effects of the metal active sites.[7c,10] The competitive interaction of H+/water with two metal centers may tune the binding strength of intermediates and control the reaction pathway to accelerate the reaction rate of CO2 reduction on the surface. A few recipes of alloying have been developed for the synthesis of Cu-based or Sn-based electrocatalysts for CO2RR, including CuPd,[11] CuPt,[12] CuAu,[10a,13] CuAg,[14] CuIn,[15] CuZn,[16] CuSn,[17] SnAg,[18] SnPd,[19] SnPb,[20] etc. For CuSn bimetallic systems as a kind of potential catalysts, previous research works have shown that the control of their composition provided a promising approach for improving the electrocatalytic properties for CO2 reduction.
[17a,b] With carbon paper as the substrate, CuSn alloy by co-electrodeposition with a ratio of 1 : 3 exhibited the highest FE of 95% for formate.[17c] The excellent electrocatalytic activity and selectivity for CuSn3 catalysts could be attributed to the positive oxidation of Sn with electron donation to Cu in the CuSn alloy. The phase and the structure can also affect the activity and the selectivity of CuSn catalysts for CO2RR. With exploiting a series of CuSn catalysts, the hollow Cu/Sn heterostructure with oxidation state exhibits promising selectivity with the FE of 70.1% for formic acid.[17d] The excellent performance was attributed to the abundant copper/tin dioxide

The spiky Cu@Sn nanocones by electrochemical coating showed the FE of 90.4% toward formate, which should be attributed to the sharp conical structure that can enrich the surface-adsorbed metal cations and promote the mass transfer.[21] By tuning the phase and the structure of CuSn catalysts, the FE of nearly 100% for formate and 91.4% for CO could even achieve by fabricated a 3D core-shell porousstructured Cu@Sn hybrid electrode[22] and Cu@Sn core-shell nanowire arrays,[23] respectively. It can be seen that the electrocatalytic performances of CuSn alloy catalysts can be affected largely by their composition, morphology and structure. However, it is still a great challenge to exclusively reveal the mechanism of CuSn alloy on the electrocatalytic CO2RR, especially the role of the surface of alloy catalysts in the reaction.
Herein, we show the electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide by CuSn alloy nanoparticles supported on the nitrogen doped graphene (NG) and investigate the mechanism of CuSn
alloy for the electrocatalytic reduction. The FE of C1 products during the CO2RR can reach nearly 93% at an overpotential at 1.0 V vs. RHE with the ratio of Cu to Sn ratio of 0.175. The alloy effect on the catalytic performance has also been studied by varying the Cu/Sn composition of CuSn NPs. The mechanism of the CuSn NPs for the CO2RR has been demonstrated through first-principles DFT calculations to understand the activity and selectivity.

In addition, the high binding energy of the metal substance to the N-doped carbon carrier can prevent the aggregation of the metal nanoparticles, therefore enhancing the stability of the catalyst. The N element doping in the NG can also significantly reduce its work function. The Mott-Schottky junction between metal and NG can increase the electron density of metal nanoparticles and improve the catalytic activity.[30]
The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image shown in Figure S1 clearly demonstrated the typical 2D structure of the NG. The CuSn NPs were loaded onto the NG by an in situ loading approach by using graphene oxide (GO) as the precursor. Typically, the GO was dispersed in dimethylformamide (DMF) by sonication to a concentration up to 0.5 mgmL 1, and following by adding DMF solution with 0.08 g Cu(NO3)2, 0.12 g SnCl4 and 0.5 g dicyandiamide. The CuSn NPs supported on NG was formed through the reduction by the hydrothermal reaction and the pyrolysis with dicyandiamide acted as the nitrogen source. Various CuSn compositions were deposited by varying the masses of Cu(NO3)2 and SnCl4 added, named as CuSnx (x indicated as the ratio of Cu to Sn).
To further verify the crystalline structure and alloy nature of the CuSn NPs, we collected X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Figure 1b–d). For CuSn0.362 NPs, the peak positions of CuSn alloy (101), (110), and (102) can be investigated at 30°, 42.8°, and 43.1° (JCPDS card no. 47-1575), respectively. The findings indicate the polycrystalline structure of CuSn NPs. The small peaks of Sn (200) at 30.5° and Sn (211) at 44.8° (JCPDS card no. 04-0673) in the CuSn NPs indicate the coexistence of the CuSn alloy and Sn phase. When the Sn content is increased in the CuSn alloy NPs, the peak intensities of CuSn alloy NPs decreased while the Sn crystalline peaks of (200), (101), (220), and (211) increase obviously. Additionally, the peak positions of CuSn (101), (110), and (102) shift to 30.2°, 43.0°, and 43.3° in CuSn0.162 in comparison with CuSn0.362, which thereby indicates the change in the lattice parameter of the CuSn alloy NPs. Therefore, the condition used in the present experiment has a dominant effect on the control of the structure, rather than the formation of alloy.[12]
The surface electronic states of CuSn alloys on NG were investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The high-resolution C 1s spectrum (Figure S2a) is deconvoluted into three subpeaks. The peaks at 284.6 eV, 285.6 eV, and 289.3 eV are assigned to C=, C N, and C=O, respectively. The appearance of the peak attributed to C N confirms the formation of the covalent bonds between graphene sheets and nitrogen. For the N 1s spectrum (Figure S2b), the peaks at 398.1 eV, 399.3 eV, 401.0 eV, and 404.2 eV are assigned to four differen t types of N (pyridinic N, pyrrolic N, graphitic N, and oxidized N).[29] The
surface of metal nanoparticles is intrinsically subjected to oxidation when exposed to air, while the bulk remains metallic because of the kinetic limit of surface oxidation.[31] The peak intensities of XPS spectra for the Cu 2p region drop when decreasing the ratio of Cu to Sn from 0.362 to 0.172 (Figure 1f). The intense Sn 3d5/2 peaks (Figure 1g) at 484.8 eV and 486.7 eV correspond to the metallic Sn0 state and the SnIV state, respectively. The peak intensity assigned to metallic Sn0
becomes much stronger by comparing with CuSn0.362, and CuSn0.162. The same trend can be detected from the Sn 3d3/2 peaks in the high energy region. This phenomenon implies that the metallic Sn phase is enwrapped by surface SnO2 layer. [19]
The morphology of as-synthesized CuSn NPs on NG was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and TEM. As shown in Figure 2a and 2b, typical SEM images show that the CuSn0.175 NPs are finely dispersed onto substrates. The obvious rough surface of NG indicates the successful decoration of CuSn NPs from the SEM image under high magnification. The morphology and distribution of CuSn0.175 NPs on NG are similar to those of other CuSn compositions (Supplementary Table S1 and Supplementary Figure S3). TEM images (Figure 2c and 2d) reveal that the CuSn0.175 NPs are homogeneously dispersed on the NG support. It should be attributed to the N doping in the substrate that can be served as the active sites for metal nanoparticle deposition and prevent their aggregation. The CuSn0.175 NPs show oval-shaped particles with the average size of about 29.1 nm. In addition, the well-defined diffraction rings shown in the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern (Figure 2e) clearly indicate the polycrystalline nature of the CuSn0.175 NPs. The ring indexed to (312), (411), (220) and (200) planes could be indexed to the Sn phase. The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image of CuSn0.175 NPs in Figure 2f clearly reveals lattice fringes with a d-spacing values of 0.205 nm, 0.278 nm, and 0.289 nm, corresponding to the planes (220), (101), and (200) of the Sn phase. However, there is no plane indexed to the phase of Cu or CuSn alloy due to the low amount of Cu atoms in CuSn0.175 NPs. With reducing the ratio of Sn to Cu, the coexistence of the CuSn alloy and Sn phase can be investigated in CuSn0.362, in agreement with the result from the XRD patterns. The results of SAED and HRTEM shown in Figure S4 and S5 display the plane (211) of Sn and the plane (110) of CuSn alloy in the CuSn0.362. It can be conformed the alloy structure in the CuSn NPs on NG. Studying electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) linear scan (Figure 2g) clearly defines the alloy structure with a higher amount of Sn, in which the EELS 2D elemental mapping (Figure 2f) determines the homogeneous distribution of Cu and Sn supported on NG. Energy Dispersive Spectrum (EDS) (Figure S6) also conforms the elemental composition of Cu, Sn, N, and C in CuSn0.175 on NG.
The electrocatalytic activity of the CuSn alloys on NG towards the CO2RR were evaluated by controlled-potential electrolysis in an H-cell filled with a CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution. The electrocatalytic activity of the CuSn alloys on NG supported on carbon paper for CO2 reduction was probed by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in CO2 or Ar-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solutions (Figure S7). The current density of the electrodes varied for each applied potential (Figure S8) and the Faradaic efficiency of the products were calculated. The results are summarized in Figure 3. For CuSn0.175 on NG catalysts, the electrolysis produces H2, CO, and formate in the potential ranging from 0.6 V to 1.2 V versus RHE and the selectivity for all the products were strongly dependent on the applied potentials. The FE of formate is 13% at 0.6 V versus RHE and the FE reaches the highest value of 53% at 1.0 V. In addition, the selectivity of C1 produces (CO and formate) is 93% at 1.0 V. Such excellent C1 produces selectivity competes with most reported Cu or Sn-based electrocatalysts (Table S3). In addition, the reduction current density remains stable for more than 15 h in 0.5 M KHCO3 with a decay less than 10% (Figure S9), confirming the remarkable stability of CuSn0.175 alloy. The change of the chemical states for Cu and Sn had been investigated by the XPS spectra (Figure S10). The spectra before and after stability tests are nearly identical, which also indicates the promising stability of CuSn0.175 on NG catalysts for the electrochemical CO2RR. The doping of nitrogen into graphene sheets results in strong binding of CuSn NPs to the NG surface, which could prevent the detachment and agglomeration of alloy NPs, thereby improving the long-term stability performance.[27] The alloy effect of CuSn NP on NG was investigated by changing the ratio of Cu to Sn. As shown in Figure 3b, the dominant product for the NG is H2 and the FE reaches 79% at 1.0 V versus RHE. The key role for the NG should mainly serve

[26] Therefore, the FE for H2 reduces to 68% and 42% for Cu/NG and Sn/NG, respectively, because of the good electrocatalytic activity of Cu and Sn reported previously. The deposition of Cu and Sn can enhance the electrocatalytic activity of CO2RR obviously. It could be found that the introducing of Sn in the CuSn NPs can improve the selectivity of C1 production of CO2RR. The FE of H2 for CuSn0.362 on NG decreases to 56% comparing with Cu on NG and the lowest FE of 7% for H2 is obtained from CuSn0.175 on NG. It is interesting that the alloy effect of CuSn can also improve the selectivity of formate. The FE of formate for Sn on NG is 54% and increases to 60% for CuSn0.162 due to the introducing of Cu in the formation of CuSn alloy. The electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) of the catalyst is an important property affecting the specific activity. The ECSA of the various CuSn alloy on NG is calculated from the cyclic voltammetry curves at different scanning speeds (Figure S11). The nuance of the ECSA obtained from the slopes indicates the similar specific activities for four
CuSn alloys on NG, which means that the efficiency and selectivity for CO2RR may be caused by the changing of the surface of the CuSn on NG by various the ratio of Cu to Sn. Benefitting from the collaboration between the CuSn alloy and the Sn metal, the electrocatalytic activity of CuSn0.175 on NG has been obviously enhanced. However, the electrocatalytic selectivity of CO and formate for the CuSn0.175 are significantly lower than those reported (>91% for CO[23] and >95% for formate[17c]). The selectivity of alloy catalysts can be affected largely by their composition, morphology and structure.[17d,21] It can be inferred that further regulation of the composition and chemical state of the CuSn alloy nanoparticles could improve the selectivity of CO or formate.
For understanding the catalytic performance of CuSn alloy, the DFT calculations were performed to reveal the intrinsic mechanisms of CO2RR processes. Three models, namely, Sn, CuSn0.362 and CuSn0.175 are constructed and geometrically optimized (the lattice parameters can be found in Supplementary Table S2). For the Sn models, the metal is tin. The CuSn0.362 and CuSn0.175 models are the CuSn alloys with different Cu to Sn ratios of 0.362 and 0.175. In the calculation, the free energy evolution profiles of HER and CO2 reduction to CO and HCOOH are calculated. As shown in Figure 4a, H2 can be easily adsorbed on the surfaces (101) and (200) of Sn, resulting from their free energies equal to 0.253 eV and 0.059 eV, respectively. After Cu is introduced, their free energies become 0.774, 0.041, 1.406 and 0.755 eV for CuSn0.362 (101), CuSn0.362 (102), CuSn0.175 (101),

The improved performance for CuSn alloy is likely due to suppressed adsorption of H. Meanwhile, more H atoms can participate in the CO2RR processes at low applied voltages, with Cu introduced into the Sn metal than those of Sn models. As shown in Figure 4b, the initial elementary steps of CO2RR are downhilled for all models and the free energies are 0.171, 0.737, and 0.578 eV for Sn (101), CuSn0.362 (101), and CuSn0.175 (101) models, respectively. The result indicates that the CuSn models show better CO2 capture performance than those of Sn models, though the Sn (101) shows the best kinetics performance among them. For Sn (101), the transition process from CO2* to COOH* is exothermic by 0.655 eV and the external potential needed to drive the transition from COOH* to CO* then to CO detached is 3.340 eV. For CuSn0.362 (101) and CuSn0.175 (101) models, the steps from CO2* transited to CO detached are uphilled and the potential barriers are 3.250 and 3.092 eV, respectively. From the results, the CuSn alloys have lower barriers than that of Sn metal which can accelerate the CO2RR process, thus the CuSn0.175 shows the highest activity by various ratio of Cu and Sn. Meanwhile, the different potential barriers of the CO and HCOOH desorption on the surfaces of Sn and CuSn alloys verify that the CuSn alloys show better selectivity than that of Sn. In addition, nonsignificant variation between the external potential in the transition to CO* and HCOOH* from COOH* leads to the poor selectivity for CO and formate comparing with the performance reported.[17c,d]

sections.heading: 3. Conclusions
sections.text: In summary, an efficient electrocatalyst was prepared by utilizing non-noble metallic Cu and Sn alloys supported on the nitrogen doped graphene for the reduction of CO2 over a wide potential range. After uniformly dispersing on NG, the bimetallic CuSn alloy NPs with an optimal composition efficiently and selectively generates CO and formate from the reduction of aqueous CO2, the highest FE of electrocatalysis by CuSn NPs for C1 products is nearly 93% at an overpotential at 1.0 V vs. RHE, which is considerably higher than that of the Cu and Sn counterparts, i. e. 32% and 58%, respectively. The DFT simulation results explain that the CuSn NPs yields higher FE because more H atoms can participate in the CO2RR and better CO2 capture performance is acquired. This study presents a strategy to provide low-cost non-noble metals that can be utilized as highly efficient electrocatalysts for the efficient aqueous reduction of CO2.

sections.heading: Experimental Section
sections.text:
Synthesis of CuSn alloy nanoparticles on nitrogen doped graphene. The CuSn alloy NPs supported on NG were synthesized via the hydrothermal method and pyrolysis. Typically, 10 mg graphene oxide powder was dispersed in 20 mL dimethylformamide (DMF) by sonication, following by adding 10 mL DMF solution with various concentration of Cu(NO3)2·2H2O, SnCl4 and 0.5 g dicyandiamide. The
mixed solution was stirred for 30 min and then transferred into 50 mL autoclave. The autoclave was placed at 200 °C for 4 h. After cooling to room temperature, the products were collected by centrifuged, and washed with ethanol and deionized water separately. The CuSn NPs on NG were obtained by annealing in nitrogen at 900 °C for 2 h after freeze drying. The total mass of Cu and Sn precursors was 0.2 g and the weight of Cu salt ranged from 0.16 g to 0.04 g (Table S1). Pure Cu and pure Sn nanoparticles on NG were also prepared as controls.
CO2 Electroreduction Measurements. Electrochemical tests were carried out in an H-shaped cell separated by a piece of Nafion 117 membrane in a three-electrode system under room temperature. Different sample mixtures were prepared by dispersing 10 mg of samples into 0.9 mL of ethanol and 0.1 mL of Nafion (5% w/w in ethanol, Alfa Aesar, USA), and were then dropped on carbon paper that was cut into 1 cm×1 cm used as working electrode. An Ag/ AgCl electrode was used as a reference electrode and a Pt film as counter electrode. The reference electrode potentials were converted to RHE using the following formula:
ERHE ðVÞ ¼ EAg=AgCl þ 0:210þ 0:0591� pH
Before CO2 reduction experiments, cyclic voltammetry (CV) was carried out in a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution (pH 7.2) for 40 cycles. All the electrochemical measurements were controlled by the electrochemical workstation (CHI 760E) at room temperature. The gas products were analyzed with a gas chromatograph equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID). The liquid products were quantified by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (Bruker AVANCE DRX 400, 500 MHz).
First-principles calculations. All first-principles-based calculations were conducted by applying the Cambridge Serial Total Energy Package (CASTEP) in Material Studio which performs the density functional theory (DFT) plane-wave pseudopotential method to carry out first principles quantum mechanics calculations. In the calculation, the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) within Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) form was used as the exchangecorrelation function. The valence states used were Sn-5s25p2, Cu3d104s1, C-2s22p2, O-2s22p4 and H-1s1. The convergence tests of the total energy with respect to the k-points sampling and the energy cutoff were carefully examined. For the lattice parameter calculation, 9×9×9 Monkhorst-Pack k-points grid and an 850 eV energycutoff were used. For the catalytic process calculations, the 3×3×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-points grid and an 850 eV energy-cutoff using for plane-wave expansion are used. In the super-cell configuration, a sufficiently large vacuum slab (about 15 Å) was maintained. The SCF tolerance was setup to 1e–6 eVatom 1 for the geometrical optimization.

sections.heading: ARTICLES
sections.text:
A wider range for reduction: We report an efficient electrocatalyst utilizing non-noble metals consisting of Cu and Sn supported on nitrogendoped graphene for reduction of CO2 over a wide potential range. The catalyst performed electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 into C1 products at a Faradaic efficiency up to 93%.
Dr. W. Xiong, J. Yang, L. Shuai, Prof. Dr. Y. Hou*, Prof. Dr. M. Qiu*, Prof. Dr. X. Li, Prof. Dr. M. K. H. Leung*
